questions.stem: Explain how early reflections on governance in India linked political authority with ethics and public welfare.
questions.answer: In India the study of politics was not treated as a separate discipline; it was closely linked to dharma, or moral duty, artha, or economic well-being, and rajadharma, the duties of the ruler. Early texts such as the Vedas, Upanishads and Puranas discuss justice, authority, social order and the responsibilities of kings and citizens, and works such as the Mahabharata and the Shukraniti address governance, law and ethical leadership. The Arthashastra, composed about 2,300 years ago, sets out how a state should be governed, how taxes should be collected, how the army should function and how rulers should ensure the welfare of the people. Power was therefore viewed as a responsibility rather than merely a privilege.

questions.stem: Name the four core disciplines that Social Science draws from in Grades 9 and 10, describe what each one studies, and explain why human society cannot be understood through any one of them alone.
questions.answer: The four core disciplines are Geography, History, Political Science and Economics. Geography studies the Earth, its environments and the relationships between people and their surroundings, asking where things are located, why they are found there and how places affect one another. History examines the human past and helps us understand how societies change over time, drawing on literary and archaeological sources. Political Science analyses systems of governance, power, and the rights and responsibilities of citizens, including constitutions, governments and institutions of the state. Economics explores how societies produce, distribute and utilise resources to meet their needs, and studies decision-making by consumers, producers and governments. No single field can fully explain human society because society is complex and its parts are connected: a drought, for example, affects crops, incomes, government relief, migration and traditional ways of coping at the same time. Each discipline asks different questions, and only together do they give a comprehensive and connected understanding.
valuePoints: Geography: the Earth, environments and people-environment relationships
History: the human past and change over time
Political Science: governance, power, rights and responsibilities
Economics: production, distribution and use of resources

questions.stem: Describe the range of sources that history writing draws on, and explain why modern historiography also uses scientific methods.
questions.answer: History writing draws on a wide range of sources. Literary and textual traditions include travelogues, memoirs, correspondence, genealogical records, folklore and oral traditions, and revenue documents. Material remains, known as archaeological sources, include monuments, architectural structures, excavated sites, artefacts, objects and art such as sculptures and paintings. Epigraphic sources are texts, decrees or records inscribed on durable materials such as stone or metal plates, and they give direct evidence about past events, rulers, administration and society. Numismatic sources are coins, currency and medals, whose metal content, inscriptions and symbols tell us about the economy, chronology, rulers, trade, political boundaries and culture. In India the itihasa-purana tradition preserved cultural memory through stories, giving cultural meaning to events and people. Modern historiography relies increasingly on empirical evidence, that is, information collected by actual observation or experimentation, and therefore uses tools such as human genetics, carbon-14 dating, archaeology and laboratory testing to establish timelines and to check what the sources say.

questions.stem: Distinguish physical, chemical and biological weathering, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: In physical weathering, rocks break into smaller pieces because of temperature changes, frost or wind, for example rocks splitting through repeated heating and cooling. In chemical weathering, minerals in rocks change because of reactions with water, air or acids, leading to new substances; substances in the air and in rain cause this. questions.stem: Explain what causes tectonic plates to move, and why most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries.
questions.answer: The movement of tectonic plates is caused by convection currents in the mantle. Heat from the Earth's core makes molten material in the mantle rise, while cooler material sinks, and this continuous movement creates currents that push and pull the plates, making them move in different directions. Plates move slowly, usually a few centimetres a year, over the semi-molten asthenosphere. Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries because it is there that plates collide, move apart or slide past each other, releasing energy and allowing magma to reach the surface. This is why they are concentrated around the Pacific Ocean, in the belt called the Ring of Fire.

questions.stem: Describe the landforms created by glaciers, both by erosion and by deposition, and explain how they are useful to human beings.
questions.answer: Glacial erosion occurs when glaciers move slowly over the land, carving and shaping it. U-shaped valleys are formed as glaciers widen and deepen river valleys. Cirques are bowl-shaped depressions at the head of a glacier, and aretes are sharp ridges between valleys. Hanging valleys occur where smaller glaciers meet larger ones, and fjords are deep, narrow inlets created when the sea floods glacial valleys. Moraines are depositional landforms made of rocks, soil and debris, called till, carried along and left behind when a glacier melts. Lateral moraines form along the sides of glaciers, terminal moraines at the end of a glacier marking its furthest advance, and medial moraines where two glaciers meet and their lateral moraines join in the middle. These landforms are useful in several ways. U-shaped valleys and cirques attract tourists for trekking, skiing and mountaineering; fjords are used as harbours and for fishing; fertile glacial soil in some valleys supports agriculture; moraines often create fertile soil and can form natural dams and lakes used for water supply, irrigation and sometimes hydroelectric power. Glaciers are also crucial sources of fresh water, feeding rivers that sustain people downstream.

questions.stem: Explain the theory of plate tectonics. In your answer describe the layers of the Earth, name the layer on which the plates move, and state what the theory helps us to understand.
questions.answer: Plate tectonics is a theory in earth science, given by W.J. Morgan, that explains the movement of the Earth's crust. According to this theory the outermost layer of the Earth is not one single piece but is broken into several large and small pieces called tectonic plates. The Earth is made up of three main layers: the crust, which is the outermost layer on which we live; the mantle below it, which is very thick and hot; and the core, the innermost layer, which is extremely hot and heavy. The crust together with the upper part of the mantle forms the lithosphere, and it is the lithosphere that is broken into tectonic plates. Beneath it lies the asthenosphere, which is semi-molten and allows the plates to move. Plates are massive slabs of solid rock that move very slowly, usually a few centimetres a year, driven by convection currents in the mantle. There are continental plates, oceanic plates and mixed plates, and major plates include the Pacific, Eurasian, African, North American, South American, Indo-Australian and Antarctic plates. The theory explains the formation of mountains, valleys, ocean basins, volcanoes and earthquakes, and the distribution of continents and oceans. It is also important for identifying earthquake-prone and volcano-prone regions and for managing the disasters that arise from them.

questions.stem: Describe the troposphere and the stratosphere, and give two differences between them.
questions.answer: The troposphere is the lowest and most important layer of the atmosphere, with an average height of about 12 kilometres. Temperature decreases with increasing altitude in it, the air we breathe exists here along with most of the water vapour and clouds, and nearly all weather phenomena such as rainfall, fog and hail occur in it. The stratosphere lies above the troposphere and extends up to 50 kilometres. It is free of clouds and weather disturbances, which makes it ideal for flying aeroplanes, and it contains a layer of ozone gas that shields us by filtering the Sun's harmful radiation, including ultraviolet radiation. Two differences are that weather phenomena occur in the troposphere but not in the stratosphere, and that the ozone layer is found in the stratosphere and not in the troposphere. The troposphere is separated from the stratosphere by the tropopause.

questions.stem: What is atmospheric pressure? Explain how differences in temperature create areas of high and low pressure, and how wind results from them.
questions.answer: Atmospheric pressure, or air pressure, is the pressure exerted by the weight of air on the Earth's surface. It is highest at sea level and falls rapidly as we go higher in the atmosphere. Horizontally, its distribution depends on the temperature of the air at a place. Where temperatures are high, air heats up and rises, creating a low-pressure area, which is associated with cloudy skies and wet weather. Where temperatures are lower, the air is cold and therefore heavy, and it sinks, creating a high-pressure area, which is associated with clear and sunny skies. Because air always moves from a high-pressure area to a low-pressure area, this difference produces wind, whose direction is also influenced by the rotation of the Earth.

questions.stem: Why does the south-west monsoon bring heavy rain to most of India while the north-east monsoon generally does not? Name the regions where the north-east monsoon is nevertheless important for rainfall.
questions.answer: The south-west monsoon, or summer monsoon, blows between June and September. During summer the landmass of India heats up faster than the surrounding oceans, creating a low-pressure area over the subcontinent while the relatively cooler Indian Ocean has high pressure. Since winds move from high to low pressure, moist winds blow from the ocean towards the land and bring rainfall. The north-east monsoon, or winter monsoon, occurs from October to February. Then the Indian landmass cools faster than the oceans, so high pressure forms over the land and low pressure over the seas, and cold, dry winds blow from land to sea, bringing no rain to most of India. However, where these winds pass over the Bay of Bengal they pick up moisture and cause rainfall on the eastern coast, especially in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and parts of Karnataka.

questions.stem: Describe the five layers of the atmosphere in order from the Earth's surface upwards, giving the main features of each.
questions.answer: The layers of the atmosphere are defined on the basis of changes in temperature and density with increasing altitude, and the density of air is highest near the Earth's surface. The troposphere is the lowest layer, with an average height of about 12 kilometres; temperature decreases with altitude, the air we breathe and most of the water vapour and clouds are found here, and nearly all weather phenomena such as rainfall, fog and hail occur in it. Above it lies the stratosphere, extending up to 50 kilometres; it is free of clouds and weather disturbances, which makes it ideal for flying aeroplanes, and it contains the ozone layer that filters the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation. The mesosphere extends up to 80 kilometres; temperature again decreases with altitude, and most meteorites entering from space burn up here. In the thermosphere, which extends from 80 to 700 kilometres, temperature rises very rapidly with altitude because gas molecules absorb X-rays and short-wave ultraviolet radiation from the Sun; it reflects radio waves back towards the Earth and helps radio transmission, the ionosphere is a part of it, and the auroras occur here. The exosphere is the uppermost layer, with very thin air, from which light gases such as helium and hydrogen float into space because gravity is weak.

questions.stem: What is precipitation? Name its forms and the main factors that affect it, and explain how local winds such as the land breeze and the sea breeze influence the climate of coastal areas.
questions.answer: Precipitation occurs when a part of the atmosphere becomes saturated with water vapour, which condenses and falls to the Earth under gravity. Its forms include drizzle, rain, snow, sleet and hail. When precipitation falls in liquid form it is called rain, which is the commonest form and lowers the temperature of a place; most groundwater is collected from rainwater, and a long absence of rainfall results in a dry climate. The main factors that affect precipitation are the prevailing winds, mountains and the seasons. Humidity is closely related to it: when water evaporates from land and water bodies it becomes water vapour, and as air gets warmer its capacity to hold water vapour increases, so humidity rises. Local winds also matter. A sea breeze blows from the sea to the land during the day, when the land becomes warmer than the sea and a low-pressure area forms over the land; a land breeze blows from the land to the sea at night, because the land cools faster than the sea. Because these two winds alternate, they are essential in creating moderate climatic conditions in coastal regions. Winds in general are named after the direction from which they blow, so a wind blowing from the west is called a westerly.

questions.stem: Describe the life of the people of Mehrgarh and explain why the site is important in the history of the Indian subcontinent.
questions.answer: Mehrgarh, on the Bolan river in present-day Pakistan, is the oldest Neolithic site of the subcontinent and its earliest agricultural village, dating back to about 7000 BCE. Its people built handmade sun-dried brick houses and granaries, buried their dead in graves, and made a variety of ornaments from semi-precious stones such as lapis lazuli and carnelian, and from shells. They cultivated wheat and barley and raised sheep, goats and Indian cattle, particularly the zebu humped bull. They were also the first to make copper objects, entering the metal age and becoming known as Chalcolithic people by about 4000 BCE. Mehrgarh is important because the Neolithic way of life that began there spread into the middle and upper Indus valley and further east, and laid the basis for the Bronze Age Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation around 3500 BCE.

questions.stem: 'The four earliest world civilisations emerged in river plains.' Explain why river plains were suited to the growth of civilisations, with reference to the civilisations described in the chapter.
questions.answer: All four of the earliest world civilisations grew up in fertile river plains: the Harappan civilisation along the Sindhu and Sarasvati, the Mesopotamian in the plains of the Euphrates and Tigris, the Egyptian along the Nile and the Chinese in the Huang He basin. River plains offered fertile alluvial soil and water, which made a surplus of food possible, and the ability to produce surplus food and material goods laid the foundation for the emergence of civilisation. In Egypt the Nile flooded every summer and left rich black mud called kemet, excellent for growing crops, and about 5000 years ago farmers learned to dig ditches to divert water into their fields and store it in reservoirs. In Mesopotamia the Sumerians were the first to build dams and canals for irrigation, and the introduction of copper tools around 4500 BCE improved farming and helped spread it across the plains. In the Indus and Ghaggar-Sarasvati basins copper tools in the fertile alluvial plains raised productivity and prosperity, and the Harappans built gabarbands across small streams and, at Dholavira, an elaborate system of dams, canals and deep tanks. Such works required collective effort, which encouraged the growth of administration and local government, as in Egypt. Rivers also carried goods and people, so Mesopotamia and the Indus and Ghaggar-Sarasvati valleys, being geographically close, developed strong contacts and trade. Rivers, however, also brought challenges such as flooding, which is why water management mattered so much.

questions.stem: Compare the Egyptian and the Chinese civilisations with reference to their rivers, the records from which we know about them, and two achievements of each.
questions.answer: The Egyptian civilisation grew along the Nile, whose annual summer flood left rich black mud called kemet on the land; Egyptians called their land Kemet, meaning 'the black'. The Chinese civilisation flourished along the Huang He, or Yellow River, and the Yangtze, whose valleys were also centres of Neolithic cultures from around 7000 BCE. Egyptian history is reconstructed from rich records: papyrus scrolls, which preserved both stories and practical details, and libraries dating back to 2000 BCE stored them in labelled jars. Greek writers such as Herodotus visited and wrote about Egypt as early as the fifth century BCE, and the script itself was read again after the Rosetta Stone was found in 1799 and deciphered by Jean-Francois Champollion in 1822. For China the earliest source of information is the oracles, symbols made on animal bones and tortoise shells that were heated until they cracked, and interpretations were made from the patterns of the cracks; later, official historiographers recorded events, so China has an abundance of historical records. Among Egyptian achievements are the calendar, developed by counting the days between the floods of the Nile, with three seasons of four months each and a year of 365 days, and the building of pyramids such as the step pyramid at Saqqara over the burial chambers of the pharaohs, together with mummification. Among Chinese achievements are the mastery of bronze metallurgy to produce weapons, tools and elaborate ritual vessels, and the carving of jade objects and figurines; silk, known from the Neolithic period, became a major item of external trade in the second century BCE under the Han dynasty, giving its name to the Silk Route, and China was the first country to introduce paper currency and to develop civil services through public examination.

questions.passage: Three of the earliest writing systems of the world began at about the same time: the pictographic script used by the Harappans on seals and pottery, the cuneiform script of the Sumerians in Mesopotamia, and the hieroglyphic script of ancient Egypt. Cuneiform was written by pressing a wedge-shaped stylus into the damp surface of clay tablets, and by 3000 BCE it was used all over Mesopotamia by different city-states even though they spoke different languages. Those tablets record great myths and epics, hymns, law codes and educational treatises, and also keep account of the work of potters, seal cutters, shipbuilders, carpenters and farm workers. The Egyptian script became readable again after a French army engineer repairing a fort in 1799 found a large black stone covered in writing of three kinds, one of them Greek, which people could still read; a French linguist deciphered the script in 1822. questions.stem: Describe how early Indian kingdoms and empires were administered below the level of the king, with reference to the divisions used between about 300 CE and 800 CE.
questions.answer: Supreme authority rested with the king, but general administration was carried out by officers working at provincial and local levels. Kingdoms were divided into provinces, which were subdivided into divisions and districts. Between about 300 CE and 800 CE power was decentralised: the kingdom was divided into provinces known as bhuktis in the north and mandalas or mandalams in the south; these were subdivided into divisions called vishaya or bhoga in the north and kottams or valanadu in the south; below them were districts, adhishthana or pattana in the north and nadu in the south; groups of villages were called vithis in the north and pattala or kurram in the south; and villages formed the lowest administrative unit. District governors, or pradeshikas, were responsible for judicial and administrative functions, and often took decisions after consulting important residents such as bankers, caravan leaders, artisans and scribes. Cities had their own governors in charge of revenue collection and law and order, and each village was led by a headman, the gramika.

questions.stem: Describe the role of guilds in the early Indian economy, and explain what the Nashik cave inscription tells us about them.
questions.answer: Guilds, or shrenis, were collective organisations of traders, artisans and merchants engaged in the same profession, craft or occupation. They played a significant part in the expansion of trade and commerce, especially after the rise of the mahajanapadas in the sixth century BCE, when metallic coins, beginning with silver punch-marked coins, also came into circulation. Guilds regulated the quality of goods and often fixed prices to protect both artisans and consumers, and supervised the conduct of their members through guild courts that enforced professional standards and discipline. The Jataka literature refers to eighteen types of guilds. The Nashik cave inscription of the second century CE, of the Shaka king Nahapana and his son-in-law Ushavadata, records that monetary donations were deposited with guilds, which were obliged to pay a fixed rate of interest on these endowments, and the interest was used to maintain Buddhist monasteries and caves. This shows that guilds were not merely associations of craftspersons and traders but also functioned as banking and credit institutions capable of investing funds securely and generating a steady income.

questions.stem: Trace the development of political organisation in early India from the janas of the Vedic period to the rise of empires.
questions.answer: Early Vedic society was organised into janas, or clans, groups of people bound by kinship ties. The Rigveda alone mentions about thirty janas, five of which, the Yadu, Turvasha, Puru, Anu and Druhyu, were together called the panchajana. In this period the raja functioned primarily as a clan chief who led the group in warfare and protected its members, and he worked alongside three assemblies, the sabha, the samiti and the vidhata. With time this organisation evolved into territorial entities called janapadas, roughly between 1000 BCE and 600 BCE, so that people were connected not only by kinship but also by belonging to a land. Control over land, agricultural production and trade routes became increasingly important and led to more complex administration. From about 600 BCE to 300 CE, larger political units called mahajanapadas arose, and the sources usually speak of sixteen of them. The political landscape now included both monarchical states, rajyas, and republican states, ganas or sanghas. Among the mahajanapadas, Magadha in present-day Bihar became the most powerful because of its strategic location, fertile plains and strong rulers, and its expansion led to the rise of the Mauryan Empire, one of the largest and most powerful empires in early Indian history, founded by Chandragupta Maurya in 321 BCE. In the Deccan the Mauryas were succeeded by the Satavahanas, and further south were the Cholas, Pandyas, Keralaputras and Satiyaputras. Later, the Guptas in the north and the imperial Cholas in the south built large empires with elaborate administrative systems.

questions.stem: What do inscriptions and other records tell us about social mobility and about the position of women in early India?
questions.answer: Varna and jati were not always rigid categories, and there was considerable mobility within and across them. Several ruling families came from diverse social backgrounds, including the Nandas, Mauryas, Shungas, Satavahanas, Vakatakas, Guptas and Pushyabhutis. The Mandsaur stone inscription of 473 CE records a guild of silk weavers who migrated from Lata in Gujarat to Dashapura in Madhya Pradesh during the Gupta period and who were skilled not only in weaving but also in archery, astrology and other occupations, which shows occupational mobility. The Karitalai copperplate inscriptions of Maharaja Jayantha, of the late fifth century CE, record brahmanas working as land managers. Early Vedic texts also show that occupations were flexible: a verse of the Rigveda describes a family in which the speaker is a poet, the father a physician and the mother a grinder of corn. On women, the Vedic period is described as one in which women held a respected position: they took part in scholarly learning, in certain contexts performed rituals, attended gatherings including the sabha, and several hymns of the Rigveda are traditionally attributed to women sages such as Apala, Vishvavara, Ghosha and Lopamudra. Later records show queens and royal women taking part in governance and religious patronage: Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, ruled as a regent in the Vakataka kingdom and issued land grants in her own name, and in the Chola period inscriptions record Sembiyan Mahadevi supporting temple building and religious institutions. Women also appear as donors in votive inscriptions from the post-Maurya period, and Sangam literature portrays women in agriculture, cattle rearing, spinning, fishing and salt production, and names poetesses such as Avvaiyar. The position of women did, however, fluctuate and at times declined as social and political conditions changed.

questions.passage: The Uttaramerur inscription of Parantaka I, of the tenth century CE, is carved in the Vaikuntha Perumal temple in the Kanchipuram district of Tamil Nadu. It describes in detail how a village assembly of the Chola period chose its members. The names of eligible candidates were written on palm leaves and placed inside a large pot. At a public gathering, often held at a temple and in full view of the whole community, a young child was asked to draw the leaves out one by one, and those drawn were selected. This was the Kudavolai, or ballot pot, system. The members elected in this way were then divided into specialised committees, called variyams, each entrusted with an important village responsibility such as managing the irrigation tank, administering justice or collecting taxes. The same inscription also specifies that a candidate for the village assembly should have honest earnings and be pure of mind.

questions.stem: Name the six Fundamental Rights guaranteed by the Constitution of India along with their Articles, and state how a citizen may seek a remedy if a Fundamental Right is violated.

Any violation of these can lead to appropriate legal action, and citizens can seek constitutional remedies under Articles 32 and 226 for the protection and reinforcement of their Fundamental Rights. questions.stem: Explain the rule of law and state why it is essential in a democracy.
questions.answer: The rule of law is a fundamental principle of any democratic society. It ensures equality before the law, which means every individual, irrespective of status, identity or rank, is treated equally by the law, and equal protection of the law, which means all persons in similar circumstances are treated equally without arbitrary discrimination. It establishes that no one is above the law. When laws are violated, disputes are resolved in a court of law through the procedure established by law and not by force or personal influence, and no citizen can be punished without following that procedure. Everyone is given a fair opportunity to defend their rights against arbitrary action. It is essential because it prevents the misuse of power, protects people's rights, and promotes justice, accountability and trust in the democratic system.

questions.stem: Compare how women obtained the right to vote in India with how they obtained it in Britain and the United States of America, and explain why the right to vote alone does not ensure equal participation.
questions.answer: In a number of countries women had to wage a long and difficult struggle to secure the right to vote. In Britain women received full voting rights only in 1928, and in the United States of America in 1920, after decades of protests and movements, so democracy in those societies expanded gradually. In India, by contrast, when the Constitution came into force in 1950 universal adult franchise was extended to all citizens, men and women alike, without discrimination, and Indian women did not have to engage in prolonged legal battles or protests to secure voting rights. However, the right to vote does not automatically ensure equal participation, because social prejudices continue to act as barriers and affect the adequate representation of women in politics. This is why the Constitution provides for reservation of not less than one-third of the directly elected seats for women in every Panchayat under Article 243(d) and in every Municipality under Article 243(t), and several states and union territories have gone further and provided 50 per cent reservation.

questions.stem: Explain the separation of powers among the three organs of government in India, and describe how checks and balances are maintained between them.
questions.answer: The separation of powers means that the work of government is divided among three organs, each with distinct responsibilities. The legislature makes laws, the executive implements them, and the judiciary interprets them. This prevents the concentration of power in any one organ and enables democratic institutions to function effectively and responsibly. The separation is essential for maintaining checks and balances. For example, Parliament has the power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, but the judiciary can review such amendments to ensure that they are consistent with the spirit of the Constitution. The executive power of enforcement agencies is regulated by laws and rules framed by Parliament and can also be reviewed by competent courts. If a law is inconsistent with the constitutional provisions, the judiciary has the power to declare it unconstitutional. The judiciary upholds the Constitution, ensures that laws enacted by Parliament and the State Legislative Assemblies are in accordance with it, and is an impartial and independent institution that safeguards citizens' rights; through initiatives such as Public Interest Litigation it has also widened access to justice. Accountability is further supported by elections, public debate, engagement with civil society, and laws such as the Right to Information Act, 2005, which allows citizens to seek information from government agencies. If one organ made the laws, implemented them and judged disputes about them, power would be concentrated and citizens' rights would have no protection.

questions.stem: 'The democratic ethos in India did not emerge suddenly.' Trace the development of democratic ideas in India from early times to the framing of the Constitution.
questions.answer: The idea of democracy has been part of the Indian ethos since early times. In the Vedic period there were assemblies such as the sabha, the samiti and the vidhata, which involved collective decision-making, and the king was not an independent ruler but worked in consultation with assemblies, ministers and officers of various capacities. Early republican states, the ganas or sanghas, also existed alongside monarchies. A verse from the Aikyamatya Suktam of the Rigveda emphasises collective thinking, shared discussion and unity of purpose, showing that consultation, consensus and shared responsibility have deep roots in India's intellectual and cultural traditions. The functioning of the Bauddha Sanghas, the monastic community established by Gautama Buddha, also reflects these traditions: the Sangha encouraged debate and discussion, and its members could choose their leader and take decisions through voting. Over the long passage of time invasions disrupted the political and social fabric of parts of the country, and by the nineteenth century the British had colonised most of the subcontinent; foreign rule altered political structures and limited people's participation in their own governance. However, the long struggle for independence revived and strengthened democratic ideas. Before independence, the Constituent Assembly was formed in 1946 to draft a constitution, and it took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to produce the world's longest written Constitution. Alongside indigenous traditions, the global spread of democratic values influenced the Constituent Assembly Debates, and the members believed the Constitution should be not a rigid legal code but a dynamic document capable of evolving through lawful amendments without compromising its fundamental values. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.

questions.stem: What is delimitation, and why is it necessary?
questions.answer: Delimitation is the process of determining the number of seats and fixing the territorial boundaries of constituencies in each state for elections to the Lok Sabha and the Vidhan Sabha. It is necessary because the boundaries of constituencies are not permanently fixed and population density shifts over time. Without delimitation one Member of Parliament might represent five lakh people while another represented twenty-five lakh, which would defeat the objective of equal representation. Delimitation aims to keep the ratio of seats to population as close to equal as possible across all constituencies. Article 82 of the Constitution mandates the establishment of a Delimitation Commission.

questions.stem: Compare the First-Past-The-Post system, the majority system and proportional representation on the basis of how a voter votes and how seats are won.
questions.answer: Under the First-Past-The-Post system each voter votes for one candidate in their constituency, and the candidate with the most votes wins even if those votes are less than 50 per cent of the total polled. Under the majority system each voter votes for one candidate, but to win a candidate must receive more than 50 per cent of the votes; if no one does, the top two candidates compete again in a second round. Under proportional representation voters vote for a party rather than a person, and seats in the parliament are allotted in proportion to the total votes received by each party, so power is shared proportionately. India elects members of the Lok Sabha and the Vidhan Sabha by the First-Past-The-Post system, while the Rajya Sabha, the President and the Vice President are elected by proportional representation.

questions.stem: Describe any three functions of the Election Commission of India.
questions.answer: First, the Commission prepares the electoral roll. It sends official enumerators to every household to collect data about eligible electors, and rolls are prepared for each constituency, organised polling station-wise; only those whose names appear on the roll may vote. It also conducts the Special Intensive Revision, updating, verifying and correcting the rolls so that no eligible citizen is left out and no ineligible person is included, and it settles claims and objections before publishing the final roll. Second, it decides the schedule and dates of elections, taking into account weather conditions, the agricultural cycle, school and university examination schedules and festivals. Third, it registers political parties and allots symbols: only registered parties may contest, it classifies parties as recognised national or state parties or registered-unrecognised parties, allots election symbols, insists that parties hold organisational elections periodically, and acts as a quasi-judicial body in disputes over recognition and symbols. It also works to ensure that elections are free, fair, transparent and inclusive.

questions.stem: State three corrupt practices or electoral offences listed in the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and explain why each would damage a free and fair election.
questions.answer: First, any gift, offer or promise made by a candidate, or with the candidate's consent, to a person in order to make them contest, withdraw, vote or refrain from voting is a corrupt practice; it replaces the voter's free judgement with an inducement. Second, appealing to people to vote or refrain from voting on the basis of religion, caste, race, community or language is an offence; it divides the electorate on identities rather than on programmes and policies. Third, candidates, or anyone acting on their behalf, are prohibited from taking assistance in favour of the candidate from government-related personnel, including gazetted officers, judges and magistrates, armed forces personnel, police personnel and excise officers; such assistance would put the machinery of the state behind one contestant and destroy the equality of the contest. If fairness is not ensured, public confidence in electoral institutions gradually weakens, and although elections are held, their democratic value is reduced.

questions.stem: Describe the Election Commission of India: what kind of body it is, how election work is organised at the state level, and the criteria by which a party is recognised as a national party or as a state party.
questions.answer: The Constitution of India vests in the Election Commission of India the superintendence, direction and control of the entire process for the conduct of elections. It is an autonomous, permanent, constitutional body established on 25 January 1950, and Articles 324 to 329 of the Constitution provide for it and define its powers and duties. It conducts elections to the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha, the Vidhan Sabha, the Vidhan Parishad, and to the offices of the President and the Vice President. At the state level, election work is supervised by the Chief Electoral Officer of the state, who is appointed by the Commission from among the civil servants in consultation with the concerned state government; various state government officers such as District Magistrates, Sub-Divisional Magistrates and Tahsildars are also assigned election duties as District Election Officers, Returning Officers and Electoral Registration Officers. A party may be recognised as a national party if it fulfils any one of three conditions: it secures not less than 6 per cent of the valid votes polled in any four or more states in a general election to the Lok Sabha or to the Legislative Assembly and in addition wins four seats in the Lok Sabha from one or more states; or it wins at least 2 per cent of the seats in the Lok Sabha with candidates elected from at least three states; or it is recognised as a state party in at least four states. A party may be recognised as a state party if, for example, it secures not less than 6 per cent of the valid votes polled at a general election to the Legislative Assembly of that state and in addition wins at least two seats in that Assembly, or wins at least 3 per cent of the seats in the Assembly or at least three seats, whichever is more. Parties that have not secured enough votes, or have never contested since registration, remain registered-unrecognised political parties.

questions.stem: 'Elections are the soul of democracy.' Explain why regular elections matter, and describe the role political parties play in them.
questions.answer: Elections are one of the most important processes for exercising democratic rights, and regular and periodic elections lie at the core of democracy. One of the most crucial elements of democracy is participating in the periodic election of those who will make decisions on our behalf. Elected representatives are accountable to the people, and the right to elect them and to hold them accountable is ensured through periodic elections; the vote is the principal means by which a citizen exercises this right. A government cannot continue beyond its prescribed term without seeking the mandate of the people again, and a contest in which only one party stands would give the voter no real choice. Elections therefore provide accountability, representation, legitimacy and equality. Political parties are essential to this system. There are often dozens of contestants in each constituency, and most belong to a party, though some contest independently. Voters learn about the candidates, their policies, their vision for development and their positions on social, economic, cultural and political issues mainly through the parties. Parties organise public opinion, campaign on specific issues, offer voters meaningful choices and enable them to make informed decisions. They present their agenda and elaborate on their promises in election rallies and through media platforms. After the election, the winning party or coalition forms the government and formulates and implements policies, while the opposition ensures accountability and participates in debates and committees. India has a multi-party system, which reflects the country's diversity of languages, cultures, religions and regions, and parties function within the framework of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

questions.passage: On polling day, Ravi went with his family to a polling station guarded by police personnel. A wheelchair had been kept ready for his elder brother, who has a disability, and volunteers guided them to the booth. The voting machine at the booth carried Braille markings. After casting his vote, Ravi was able to see the slip printed by the Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail. His eighty-nine-year-old grandmother had not come with them; she had voted from home, a facility extended across India for the first time during the 2024 General Elections to senior citizens above 85 years of age and to persons with disabilities having a benchmark disability of 40 per cent. Ravi's cousin, posted far from home with the armed forces, had received his postal ballot electronically and had voted from where he was stationed.

parts.prompt: Which system did Ravi's cousin use to vote, and for whom was it developed?
parts.answer: He used the Electronically Transmitted Postal Ballot System, ETPBS, which was developed for service voters so that they can receive and cast their postal ballots electronically from anywhere outside their constituency.

parts.prompt: Name two steps described in the passage that made this election more inclusive, and explain why such steps matter for a free and fair election.
parts.answer: Two such steps are the wheelchair and volunteers provided for a person with a disability together with Braille markings on the voting machine, and the facility of voting from home for very senior citizens and persons with a benchmark disability; the electronic postal ballot for service voters is a third. (1 mark for any two) These matter because if some citizens face difficulty in exercising their right to vote because of accessibility, then although the election is held, its democratic value is reduced; making the process inclusive, impartial and trustworthy is what maintains public confidence in it.
